common_name: Big Time Blue Lavender (Compact Deep Blue English Lavender)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; this compact selection is well suited to container culture.

directions: Big Time Blue is a dwarf English lavender bred for pot and edging use, forming a tight, rounded mound of narrow silvery foliage topped with unusually large, dark blue-purple flower spikes for its small size. It blooms earlier than many standard-height English lavenders and tends to repeat if lightly sheared after the first flush. Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil, since like all lavenders it is intolerant of wet feet and rich, heavy soils that promote root rot and floppy growth. Its compact habit makes it a strong choice for patio containers, rock gardens, and the front of a sunny border where larger lavender cultivars would overwhelm the space.

common_name: Blue Cushion Lavender (Dwarf Mounding English Lavender)

planting.note: Transplant rooted cuttings after the last frost into lean, well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Blue Cushion forms an exceptionally dense, low, rounded mound of fine silvery-green foliage, living up to its name as one of the tightest-growing English lavender cultivars available. Slender deep violet-blue flower spikes rise just above the foliage in a tidy, uniform flush, making this a favorite for edging, knot gardens, and mass plantings where a neat, consistent shape matters. Plant in full sun in gritty, fast-draining soil and avoid overwatering or fertile soil, both of which loosen the naturally tight habit and invite root rot. Shear lightly right after bloom to preserve the cushion form and encourage dense new growth for the following season.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; Grappenhall is one of the oldest and most vigorous lavandin cultivars, grown since the early twentieth century.

directions: Grappenhall is a large, vigorous lavandin prized for its broad mound of long, wide grey-green leaves and tall, gracefully arching stems topped with pale lavender-blue flower spikes among the longest of any lavandin cultivar. Like other lavandins it inherits improved heat and humidity tolerance from its spike lavender parentage, making it more forgiving than pure English lavender in hot, muggy climates. Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained to dry soil, spacing generously to allow its broad, billowing form to develop without crowding. Shear back hard after flowering to keep the substantial size in check and prevent the woody, splayed-open habit lavenders develop with age.

planting.note: Transplant rooted starts after last frost into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; propagated by cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Fathead earns its name from its unusually large, plump flower cones, noticeably oversized compared with most Spanish lavender cultivars, crowned with showy upright purple bracts above aromatic silvery-green foliage. It flowers heavily from mid-spring into summer and often reblooms if deadheaded promptly after the first flush fades. Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil, since it shares the family's low tolerance for wet feet, humidity, and heavy clay. Its well-branched, rounded habit and bold flower heads make it a strong container or border-front specimen where its oversized blooms can be appreciated up close.
